utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, The Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Matthew Olmsted for the Prosecution, joined by Matthew Gillett; Case Manager, Thomas Laugel; and our intern, Maggi Qerimi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell, with Jolana Makraiova, our intern. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness may be brought in. Mr. Gosnell, do you expect to need more time than today's hearing?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Brigadier Wilson. May I remind you that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please proceed, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You first met Goran Hadzic as you testified yesterday or the day before, on the 27th of January, 1992. Do you recall what position he held at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: My -- I don't know the exact title, but I understood he was the most senior political representative of Sector East area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So you do recall this was before the area encompassed by Sector East had joined the RSK; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you recall that the Geneva Accords were signed by -- on the Serbian side, General Kadijevic for the JNA and President Milosevic for the Republic of Serbia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You don't know that the two parties on the Serb side to the Vance Plan were the JNA and the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who signed the agreement. My understanding is responsible political authorities on both sides signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, leaving aside the exact identities of who did the signing, do you recall that the parties on the Serb side were the JNA and the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said I didn't know who signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were you having separate discussions with the JNA during your first visit to Belgrade during this interval between the 26th of January to the 30th of January?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a meeting with the minister of defence, the senior military man, immediately after the meeting we had with Mr. Kosic. I think that was on the 26th. And, yes, there were many discussions in my role as UNMLOY, where we talked to the JNA and -- and while I may have met political representatives from Sector East in that UNMLOY period, I don't recall that I remember meeting JNA representatives in the Sector East area during the UNMLOY time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: In Belgrade, do you remember whether you met General Kadijevic or any very senior member of the JNA - I'm not talking about the minister of defence - Kadijevic or other senior member of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were lots of generals present at these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But you never met separately with the JNA officers. Are you saying you were always meeting JNA officers in the presence of a political official from Serbia at least?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I can't recall the exact composition of the delegation. There were maybe a dozen people sitting on the other side of the desk, and -- I've done well on occasions to remember who the principal was, let alone his assistants.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That's understandable, Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we bring up L2, please, Defence tab 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, sir, just looking at the front page of this document, do you remember that this was the bundle of documents that, together, reflected the Vance Plan as you understood that to be the case in January 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 8 of this document, please. And by page 8, I mean e-court page 8. If we look down at the bottom of paragraph 25 -- and we mentioned this yesterday, Brigadier, but I would just like to take us to the text specifically. It's referring to constructive negotiation -- an effective cease-fire would further open the way for constructive negotiations between the representatives of the republics, refers to a declaration of the 12-member states of the European community at Rome on 8 November 1991. That declaration stated inter alia that: "The prospect of recognition of the independence of those republics wishing it can only be envisaged in the framework of an overall settlement. The conference has also, with the agreement of its participants, ruled out any changes in external or internal borders by means of force. I believe that any selective uncoordinated departure from those principles could hold very serious dangers, not only for the republics of Yugoslavia, but for all of her peoples ..." Now, this reflect, does it not, the UN position that -- and the date of this again is the 11th of December, 1991, that there should be no unilateral declarations of independence by the republics?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't know without -- seriously without re-reading this document in -- in detail. I -- I couldn't speculate on that what the intent of the author was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we could go, please, to page 11 of e-court, paragraph 8. And now we are inside the Vance Plan itself, Brigadier. And at paragraph 8, it says: "As already stated, the special arrangements in these areas," and this is referring to the UN protected areas, "would be of an interim nature and would not pre-judge the outcome of political negotiations for comprehensive settlement of the Yugoslav crisis." Now, do you remember that upper-most in the mind of the Serb side was the significance of this provision, namely that what they had secured was a -- an assurance that the final status of the protected areas was a matter for future negotiation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They certainly expressed that view. Whether it was the most important to them, I can't speculate on. But certainly they expressed that view.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And -- and when I say "status," I mean the question as to whether or not those protected areas would ultimately be absorbed into a future or, as it became the case by the end of 1991, an existing Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was certainly their negotiating position.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, yesterday at page 7439 of the transcript, you were asked about your recollections of that meeting with Mr. Hadzic on the 27th of January, and you had the following exchange with the Prosecutor, "Do you recall" -- this is the question: "Q. Do you recall Mr. Hadzic's response to the issue of intimidation on this occasion? "A. I -- I can't recall the detail of the conversation. It's 20 years ago. But the central theme of the discussion was the impossibility of the -- the Serbs living in the UNPA again to be able to live under, with Croats, but in particular under any Croat political sort of governments and also the provocation that the Croat forces were conducting, which was creating an insecure and threatening environment, at least along the confrontation lines. He was generally pleading that it would be very difficult to reach s political accommodation after some time." Now, am I right in understanding that the answer that you have described there as having been given, or the remarks having been given by Mr. Hadzic, was he addressing those remarks to the issue as -- of whether the Serb protected areas would be reabsorbed into Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you quote -- I'm sorry to be difficult but it's important to my answer. When you quote what the Prosecutor asked me, it relates on an occasion. I'm not quite sure what that occasion was, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This --

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you -- you might need to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: In context to this occasion it was the 27th of January, 1992 [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, okay. Okay. And, sorry, the end of your question again?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, do you recall that he was addressing those remarks to whether the protected areas were going to be reintegrated into Croatia? Was that what he was addressing in his comments?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I believe he was addressing the general situation. It was a concern about what the situation would be with UNPROFOR on the ground and where this would possibly lead to and general concerns about the political situation rather than anything specific. But, as I say, I'm recalling a general theme of a discussion, not -- not -- not a -- I can't vouch for precise wording.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That's fair enough. I'm trying to get to the gist of it, really.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And here you have used in your answer the word "impossibility" of the Serbs living in the UNPAs being able to live under, with Croats.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So what was he saying was impossible? Wasn't he saying that what was impossible was the idea of the protected areas being reintegrated into Croatian republic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was saying he could not foresee a circumstance where the Croat nation and the Serb nation could live, intermingle, and together again. They would need to live separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did he express to you the view, and you testified that by this state there were few non-Serbs still living in the protected areas, did he express to you the view that the non-Serbs should be segregated from the Serbs in the protected areas?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was talking to Mr. Goulding. I was a witness, so -- Mr. Goulding was the principal, but I don't recall any discussion about segregating within the UNPA.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did he express the view to you, to Mr. Goulding, or to anyone else that those few remaining non-Serbs should be harassed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't -- well, I have no recollection of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection whether he expressed the view to you, Mr. Goulding, or to anyone else that they should be forced out of the protected areas?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that at all either, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to move now to show you some documents about the special police, some of which you may have seen before and some of which you may not have seen before. But I just want to preface some of these questions by telling you that I'm going to show you documents from the United Nations. These are not documents from other sources, and I don't intend to suggest to you that the information is always entirely accurate, but I want to ask you some questions about whether you saw these documents and what they indicate to you. Could we have P2414.2398, which is Defence tab 65. And perhaps I should follow up on my previous line of questioning with one additional question in respect of what Mr. Hadzic said to you on the 27th of January. In respect of the questions I asked you about segregation or harassing or forcing non-Serbs out of the protected areas, did he ever express any of those views any of the other occasions that you met him in 1993 in the context of the negotiations in New York or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, in front of us, we have a document from the civil affairs co-ordinator in Sector East to Mr. Thornberry. And this is the 22nd of June, 1992. And if we could turn to page 3 in e-court. Actually, we need to start on page 2. Now, there at the top it refers to political meetings during the period between the 15th and 21st of June. And it says on the 16th June, the sector commander introduced the CCAO and colleagues to a meeting of heads of the opstinas of the Baranja officers and professionals in local government. Present were some 200 persons, including Mr. Vezovic ... Mr. Spanovic (Defence), et cetera." If we go over to the next page, at the very top: "This meeting which ended at 1400 hours presented Colonel Jokin, civil affairs and CIVPOL with the opportunity to express UNPROFOR's concern and delay at the local level of phase 2 of the peace plan, and insisted that the special police ... should be disbanded to outline the horrendous atrocities that are being committed by the milicija and Red Berets against old persons and other minorities and express indignation at the barbarous nature of the society and the lack of control over these criminal elements. Mr. Spanovic stated that the police were fighting a war, that a special police force was needed but that all others will be disbanded as per plan. As regards the composition of the police, Spanovic conceded that the police force is probably larger than needed but as the situation stabilises, the force will be decreased. He added that the timing also depended on UNPROFOR." Now, I just have a few questions to ask you about this. First of all, do you remember whether you saw this particular document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no recollection of it at all. At this time I was in Sarajevo. And this is an internal civil affairs document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you don't remember whether the Prosecution showed this document to you during the preparation of your statement in 2012 or in your preparation for your testimony here?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no recollection of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What is your understanding, if any, of the relationship between the Red Berets and the special police?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they were separate entities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Who commanded the Red Berets, according to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Who was the ultimate authority over the Red Berets, according to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they came from Serbia proper and operated throughout the UNPAs and Bosnia on an as required basis. And I -- my understanding at the time was when they operated within those area, they operated in there with the agreement, if not the support of the local political authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: When did they arrive in the UNPAs, according to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is they were there from the time I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that Mr. Spanovic here appears to be rather frankly acknowledging the role of the special police? In other words, he's not concealing that their true function is, indeed, to be a fighting force rather than to be merely policemen directing traffic at intersection, for example.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that here we see Mr. Spanovic suggesting that there is the special police, whom he is saying are duly designated to carry long-barrelled rifles or perform this function of protecting the areas whereas there are other elements who would be, as he says, disbanded as per plan?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what he says in the statement, or this record of his statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And that last part where he says the timing depends on UNPROFOR, do you understand him -- and I'm asking you to, if you can, provide an answer based upon your information from your other conversations with Serb interlocutors. Would you understand him to be saying here that he is awaiting or expects a robust UNPROFOR presence as a precondition for reducing the size of that force?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He -- he could mean that. I think ultimately he means that he'll take action when he believes there's a secure environment that allows him to reduce or disband his special police.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 05197, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could we get the tab, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Defence tab 72.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Brigadier, this is a -- another communication between the civil affairs co-ordinator for Sector East and Mr. Thornberry. And we're going here in more or less chronological order. This is the 2nd of July, 1992. Do you recall whether you saw this document at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I have no recollection of whether it's an internal civil affairs document. There's no reason I would see it, unless Mr. Thornberry referred it to me or it was covered in a conversation. But at a quick glance at the first paragraph, it is fairly typical of correspondence at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 7, please. Now, we're going to come to paragraph -- subparagraph (b) but let me just start by asking you something about subparagraph (a) while we have it here on the screen. It refers to a 67-year-old Croatian lady being forced to leave her house. The house was taken over by a refugee family: "Civil affairs officer met with the commander of the local police and demanded the return of the lady to her house. She feels insecure and requested the assistance of UNPROFOR to leave the Baranja." Now we don't have a lot of details here, Brigadier, but was it common -- we referred earlier to many non-Serbs having remained behind being elderly. Was it your impression that they were left behind without the rest of their families in many cases?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And that would place them already in a position of vulnerability, would it not, to be separated from their families in that fashion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Particularly in the culture of the Balkans where family support structures are so important; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And so there might already be an inclination, even leaving aside any threats or inducements to leave, to want to leave and rejoin the remainder of the family; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And if someone comes around to the house and issues verbal threats or shoots a bullet into the roof, in most cases that's going to be sufficient to want to induce the person to leave, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true. There are many ways to intimidate old people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And the result at least in this particular case is that the person comes to UNPROFOR and says, Please help me leave; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, my understanding is that UNPROFOR's position on this is a bit delicate in a situation of this kind. On the one hand, they do want to safe-guard the lives and security of people, if necessary, by allowing them or facilitating their departure. On the other hand they're very sensitive to be being accused of ethnic cleansing themselves by the Croatians. Isn't that a fair summary of the dilemma facing UNPROFOR at this time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And, again, just looking and focussing on this particular case, which -- which, I suggest, is not atypical, it's going to be very difficult for UNPROFOR to post a soldier in the front yard of this lady to ensure that events such as a bullet being fired into the roof or verbal harassment or other forms of cohesion don't occur; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true. It's much more difficult to deal with a thousand of these cases, provide security for a thousand, and at least to attempt to address the root cause of the situation which is the insecure, intimidating environment that existed in the UNPAs. And that's quite correctly where the emphasis should be, solving the bigger issue by at the same time ignoring the real threat to people. You have to help them if you can. Life's more important than property.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And the local police would have the same challenge that UNPROFOR would have in the sense that they probably don't have the resources to place someone in the front yard of this person's house to ensure there are no verbal threats or acts of harassment, such as a bullet being fired?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were even fewer local police than UNPROFOR people, but UNPROFOR's concern was that, really, the local police were not taking appropriate action at all. They were by all reports, in effect, aiding and abetting this process.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: When you say "aiding and abetting this process," you mean actively encouraging it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were assisting in it or ignoring it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, those are somewhat two different things.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the circumstances and the occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Entirely. And perhaps we should stick with specifics, so I'll -- I'll just take us down to subparagraph (b), if I may.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: "Mr. Stojanovic, the mayor of the village who is influential, as well as his wife who deals with refugees, has promised to assist in calming down the tension in the village. They recognised the existence of extremists who get drunk and terrorise the people during the night. The mayor stated that the Blue Brigades (special police or milicija) are involved in cases of harassment. Their commanders are requested to reorganise them and remove those who misbehave. He also mentioned that all local officials in the Baranja had received clear instructions from high officials of the Krajina to that effect." Now, was there some kind of a division in views amongst local mayors and whoever in this case is representing the Blue Brigades of the milicija?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just don't know the answer to that, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, what we have, it seems, is an accusation by a mayor that some police are involved in acts of harassment. But he also says we have received instructions from the RSK leadership -- well, high officials of the Krajina, that that should not occur. Did you hear that there were conflicting instructions of this nature?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, this is the first time I've read anywhere or heard a report similar to this where a local authority acknowledges directions from higher in regard to the security situation. I'd also point out what people say and what people are two entirely different things. It is quite common to receive assurances from a person in authority and then to find out that absolutely nothing is done about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say this is the first time you've heard of a local authority acknowledging directions from a higher --

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: In respect of security?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: For the record, this is P2416.2398. Could we have 5211, please; Defence tab 73.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Again, we have another report from civil affairs co-ordinator Sector East to Mr. Thornberry. The date is 21st of July, 1992. It refers -- appears to be the minutes of a meeting of the 20th of July. If we turn the page, meeting between Mr. Thornberry and Mr. Spanovic at Sector East headquarters on 20 July. Mr. Thornberry welcomes the guests, recalls UNPROFOR's mandate which is based on the Vance Plan, says that resolution had the force of law. Is it correct that UNPROFOR viewed the Vance Plan as, indeed, prevailing law if there was any conflict with any local legal provisions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not an interpretation I would make. The Vance Plan is an agreement between two parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: In your role as a senior member of UNPROFOR and the commander of the observer force, did you instruct your officials that the Vance Plan prevailed over any claims by anyone else that there was some contrary provision -- provision of law that prevailed.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a very broad statement. No, no, I didn't make that -- at all, that statement at all, or issue that policy, or direct my troops. The reality is that the Vance Plan had specific provisions. They were agreed by the parties and that was the guide-line for UNPROFOR and, I believe, the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Second paragraph continues to reflect what Mr. Thornberry says, apparently. And he says ostensibly that: "According to the Vance Plan police will carry side-arms only; and other armed elements would be disarmed." He reassured in the next paragraph Mr. Spanovic that UNPROFOR was capable of protecting the borders while the local authorities dealt with other problems of restoring law and order. He cautioned that the continued presence of long arms could only provoke problems, especially of infiltration, not cure them. And Spanovic responds, apparently, that the Vance Plan should be revised to take into account changes that had occurred since its adoption and one of the changes he cites is that the Republic of Krajina has no physical contact with Yugoslavia. The Bosnian component had not been foreseen and Croatia is now a new state. He proposed that the police structure should remain in all UNPAs under the mandate of the so-called Republic of the Krajina. There would be two types, two kinds of units as in the rest of the world with the following responsibilities. And then if we turn the page, he sets out the distinction between the regular milicija and the special milicijas. Now, again do we see here in this document that Mr. Spanovic is being very upfront and frank about the existence of the special police, where they are, what their role is?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And Mr. Thornberry is objecting to -- to -- in the earlier paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, let's see what the rest of the minutes reveal. At the bottom it says, "Milicija," and this appears to be Spanovic's views being expressed: "Milicija can be organised to control infiltration, the danger of which still exists. After this condition passes long weapons will be kept in HQ units where UNPROFOR can access them at any moment. The units will then be transported to special places and the APCs and vehicles garaged. They will be called upon to intervene only at the request of UNPROFOR and at infiltration of special units. They will be used after UNPROFOR is informed and will be comparable to the system of Territorial Defence weapons under UNPROFOR control." Now, do you agree especially in that last sentence but also in terms of what he is concretely proposing, is he saying that the special police should be treated in the same way as the Territorial Defence would be treated under the Vance Plan in terms of demobilisation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he is laying out special circumstances for the special police and indicating what could happen to them in the future under -- under conditions that the Serb authorities would seek to establish. But we did not believe at the time that such statements were genuine statements, that there was any genuine intention to carry this type of action out. We believe they were just delaying statements. Because, in the end there was no action taken despite vigorous representations, continuing representations for many months. They are hollow words. That's basically what I'm trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let's turn the page, please: "The director of civil affairs remarked at on the frankness of the statement and pointed to the many problems it is posed for UNPROFOR. He recapitulated the relevant part of the plan and noted that he detected an important step in Mr. Spanovic's proposal but that weapons should be under the same double-lock system as those of the Territorial Defence." Now at least it seems that Mr. Thornberry's view is that the proposal being made by Mr. Spanovic, and I entirely understand what you said about it being insincere, but Mr. Thornberry's view is that what Mr. Spanovic is trying to do, sincere or not, is to bring the special police within the parameters of the provisions that govern the Territorial Defence under the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or you could interpret it that he is not excluding this development and using it as a positive step in the right direction and he is not trying to discourage Mr. Spanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Next page, please, down at the bottom. Essentially what goes on between these two passages is a back and forth about modalities and disagreements as to whether it does comply or doesn't comply with the Vance Plan. And down at the bottom, Spanovic says that: "No one should carry arms in the zone. Enforced security was in question. While UNPROFOR has been given a mandate, it does not have enough soldiers to efficiently cover the situation. He asked whether the numbers existed. He repeated that there was a war in progress. This was not foreseen in the Vance Plan." Now, you know that in July 1992 there were infiltrations by Croat forces into Sector East, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And UNPROFOR didn't have enough soldiers to stop those incursions, did they?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So Mr. Spanovic's assessment here is correct.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And just one last item to look at with this document on the next page. There's someone named Superintendent Vranic, who is the milicijaman from the Beli Manastir. And he apparently says during this meeting that there are bunkers --

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, whereabouts in the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's the third-last paragraph from the bottom just below the part where it says "Spanovic agreed."

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And it says the milicijaman from Beli Manastir Superintendent Vranic claimed he had proof of incursions of the Croatian side into the Baranja for up upwards of 3 kilometres along the Drava river and Torjanci and Sarvas and Bilje. Let me just stop there. Did you ever hear that there were incursions of that magnitude?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a magnitude of distance, it's not a magnitude of force.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes, of that distance?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh. No, it's not surprising at all, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: There are bunkers 4 kilometres inwards within 1 kilometre from the Serbs. He asked whether Colonel Jokin has so reported. He pressed for the stay of the demilitarisation of the milicija before the Croatian side has moved. He remarked that Colonel Jokin had reinforced the activities of BelBat (APCs night and day) where it was not necessary which only confirmed his contention that the Croatians had encroached. Now, here we see, do we not, a criticism of BelBat battalion not because of harassment of Serbs at check-points or other matters, we see criticism of BelBat arising from Mr. Vranic's perceived perception that they were failing to provide adequate protection in this area?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the implied criticism, yes. But we previously agreed there was perhaps an issue of lack of numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, I don't mean to pin any specific blame or attribute blame to any one person by any means. It's a function of the situation. It's a fact --

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a fact, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And isn't the essential fact they are under-resourced to provide the protection necessary?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But we go back to the point yesterday that it was never intended that UNPROFOR would do anything more than supervise the demilitarisation of the UNPAs and then once it was demilitarised then to ensure the continuing security of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May I tendered this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry, it's already tendered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- as P2424.3978. Could we have 5228, please, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And just remind ourselves the last document was the 21st of July. This document is the 25th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could we have a tab, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Prosecution tab 156.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This is from HQ -- HQ UNPROFOR Zagreb to various sectors. Could we go to page 1, please. And it's -- appears to be a military information summary document which we've seen several examples of this during your direct testimony: "This summary as usual contains the latest info on CA, JNA, and other groupings in UNPAs and in pink zones." Could we please go to page 4. If we can go down to item 4 A: "After the harvest gathering killing incidents in Markusica, 13 August 1992, Mr. Vranic," and that's the gentleman who we saw in the last document, "local militia leader in Baranja has ordered his men to carry rifles again. He also mentioned the existence of a reserve police which is also allowed to carry rifles, but wearing civilian clothes." Now, first of all, do you remember anything about an event at Markusica on the 13th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you ever hear in the Baranja region that around this time, three or possibly four Serb farmers were killed while harvesting?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have and it doesn't surprise me, but I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And can we see here that what UNPROFOR is observing is that that caused at least some elements of the police to start carrying long-barrelled rifles again?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, who is this reserve police that is being referred to? Is that part of the special police or is it something else?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, counsel. There were many different forms of police.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: For the record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, I suppose it's a detail, but when you draw the conclusion that some elements of the police, that caused some -- at least some elements of the police to start carrying long-barrelled rifles again. In the text, I read that the carrying rifles again is about the militiamen -- the milicija, sorry, which are, I suppose, it's a paramilitary group; right? Leaded -- headed by Mr. Vranic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I should direct that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And thank you, Mr. President. I hadn't focussed on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Brigadier, when you see a reference to -- and here the words used in English are local militia, but in the previous document we saw that he was something else. When you see the words local militia in this context what do you understand that to mean?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand it to be the TDF, the Territorial Defence Force, which was volunteer organisation which was meant to take off their uniforms, hand over their rifles, demobilise. It goes back to my evidence yesterday, Your Honour, where I said this is mid-August, Sector East was only taken over by UNPROFOR in mid-July. People are coming together? There's not standard terminology. There's non -- non-native English speakers writing reports, so many different terms are being used. In regards to arming, I think -- the first sentence refers to the militia carrying rifles. The second sentence refers to the police carrying rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So you think that this is a Territorial Defence person, Vranic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't know about the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about the incident. The reason I asked you that question is because you say at the beginning of your last answer: I understand it to be the TDF. So --

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Does that mean that your understanding is that Mr. Vranic is a commander in the TDF?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what this report says, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let's go back to the previous document then, please, which is 65 ter 5211. Let's go to the last page, please. If we could zoom in, "local authorities." Down there at the bottom it says, "Vranic SUP. Beli Manastir." Does that mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not on my screen yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm looking for the very last page of 5211.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would interpret that to mean superintendent, a policeman. Of course, it is possible that somebody could belong to both organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, I -- I remember seeing Mr. Vranic being qualified in the text of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Quite right. I was just looking for the page. It's -- it's page 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we could go, please, to page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The reference here says, "The milicijamen from Beli Manastir --

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, where are you reading, please, counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry, right under "Spanovic agreed."

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: "The milicijamen from Beli Manastir, superintendent Vranic, claimed he had proof," et cetera et cetera. Does that confirm your view that in fact that is somebody who is part of the regular or local police.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, successfully confused me. He goes by the title superintendent. He is a policeman but they referred to him -- it's this confusion, lack of standardisation in terminology that we addressed yesterday. Is he here a militia or a TDF person or is he policeman? It is quite possible, as I said, that somebody could under normal circumstances wear a military uniform but when a military threat exists he could take off his police uniform and put on his green uniform. It's quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I don't disagree with you at all that there is a lack of standardisation, but what we see in these two documents which I find interesting is on the one side we have the civilian UNPROFOR authorities. I suggest to you correctly identifying this individual as local police and we have the military information summary incorrectly identifying him, at least on your interpretation, as someone in the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this sentence on -- on the screen describes him as a -- I don't speak Serbo-Croat but my interpretation is a militiaman, second word.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I just note perhaps his prior answer. The Brigadier -- it is recorded here and I think he might have misspoke. It says, "Circumstances wear a military uniform but when a military threat exists he would take off his police and put on a green uniform." Could we just correct that? Just -- I think it's a bit unclear. What were they wearing before and what would they take off.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: My learned friend is more than welcome to explore that on a re-direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It's -- it's -- it's clarifying the record, I think. It's not really something that I need to go back over in re-examination. If you could just ask the witness to look at that answer and correct what is recorded there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What did you mean, Brigadier, if can you help us?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stumbled over my answer there. It is taking off the police uniform and putting on a green militia uniform when a significant military threat emerges. I believe it is quite possible for a policeman to be a policeman in normal circumstances but also a member of the military reserve, the TDF.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Before that intervention the last thing you said was that I don't speak Serbo-Croat but my interpretation is --

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Militiaman of the second word in that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And do you interpret that to mean that he is militia in the English sense of the term?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You never heard it said that milicija, in Serbo-Croat, is a reference to police?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Very easy to properly identify the affiliation of people on the ground, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: It's very hard to properly identify the affiliation of people on the ground in these circumstances, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. And in some cases people went to considerable lengths to make it difficult to recognise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And in some cases there are errors or discrepancies in different documents as to the affiliation; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gosnell, I believe that the question you addressed to the witness concerning the difficulty in knowing to whom this and that force in the field belonged to applies to me equally on the Bench. I have the same difficulty because we are using different terms without those terms being defined previously. For instance, on page 17 of today's transcript, Mr. Spanovic made a statement concerning various types of militia, regular militias and special militia -- that is to say, milicija. At the same time, the witness speaks about Territorial Defence Forces, TDF or TO. And the -- at the same time, we are talking about the police, in English, and even the police reserves, and finally about the Red Berets. Would it be possible to have all these terms explained either through the witness or by the CLSS, by the language services. What do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I share entirely the concerns, but I'm not sure that I am in any position to resolve them, neither as to methodology nor as to substance. And I recognise that that means there is ambiguity created even in the answers of the Brigadier. I have been now, Your Honour, attempting to explore just one component of this, to try to at least understand what the nature of the difficulty is. But given -- given what this witness just said, I don't know how much further I can explore it, other than to go through some of the documents, and that's what I propose to do, in order to show or put to the witness some different terminology and see what he knows about it, if -- with Your Honours' leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I hope that you will succeed because, ultimately, we have to know who is meant when we talk about certain forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I couldn't agree more, and that's part of the Prosecution's burden of proof, I suggest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: At least I think that one confusion is put aside about -- about this specific group of which Mr. Vranic was the leader. In none of those documents, they -- this group seems to be qualified as paramilitary. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, in the two documents we've looked at, I think that's a correct statement depending on your definition of paramilitary. I'm sorry -- I -- I -- but -- I don't really see, Mr. President, that I should necessarily have to come up with that -- the reason I don't want to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yeah. My position, to be very clear, is that Mr. Vranic is part of the regular police. But the witness thinks otherwise, and that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's on the record, so let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 5226, please. Prosecution tab 131.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This is from an UN CIVPOL chief of operations dated 20th of August, 1992, to Mr. Thornberry. I suppose you wouldn't have seen this at the time either, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing it since?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've not seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we turn the page. It is talking about the Red Berets, refers to them as the Red Beret army. They appear to be involved in numerous crimes and dirty dealings and refuse to deal with CIVPOL claiming they are military in nature. And then it describes at least one crime of a Red Beret, alleged crime of a Red Beret in Ilok. We are trying to get the woman to report to police. Now, is that reflective of a common difficulty, namely, that you have someone reputed to be part of a fearsome military group, commits a crime, the victim doesn't want to go to the local police?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite a common situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Paragraph 4 is what I'm really interested in: "In Ilok it had been learned that one Sabados Joza was arrested by members of the special police (Red Beret) for singing a Croatian song. The matter is being taken up with local police who are trying to deal with the Red Beret." Now, I think earlier you said that -- and perhaps I have to ask you again, do you think the Red Berets are part of the special police or do you think they are separate?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I have to object to this question because it's a bit misleading. This witness does not know who the Red Berets were, who they were associated with, and we do have evidence as to who the Red Berets were. It was -- it's -- it was colloquial name for a unit, and I won't specify the name [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I'm going to object to any substance, otherwise the witness should be asked to excuse himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. And I won't go into the substance, but it is a misleading question. If Your Honours can understand where I'm going with it. In order to answer that question the witness would have to know more about who the Red Berets were and what their perhaps other titles could have been. And if I'm not clear, Your Honour, I could ask the witness to be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think -- I think it's -- it's clear enough. And I don't see any problem for the witness to answer whether he knows or not if the Red Berets were part of the special police or not. So I'll allow it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't believe they were part of the special police. I say it indicated my early evidence. I thought they came from outside the UNPAs and operated with the agreement of the local political authorities. Whether that's correct or not, I don't know, but that's what I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Doesn't seem to be shared by the author of this report at least in respect of that individual, does it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that's what's written there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May I tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D92, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 03624, please. If we could go to page 3 of this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You've been shown this document at least once, I think actually twice now. If we could go to page 3. And this is the Secretary-General's further report of the 28th of September, 1992, paragraph 6, "In Sector East, other armed elements" -- hopefully we can zoom in on paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could we look at the B/C/S version on the screen as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: "In Sector East, other armed elements reportedly controlled by unidentified persons in Belgrade add to UNPROFOR's problems." Now, what armed elements do you have any knowledge of that were controlled by persons in Belgrade that were present in Sector East?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of people who worked for Arkan used to appear in Sector East and other parts. It would be one example. But I'm not sure what the -- sure of the detail that the author is referring to here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could the reference have been the Red Berets, based on the information that you have?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speculate on that, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we please go to 1304, please. Now, this as it comes up on the screen is a press briefing provided by Cedric Thornberry on the 1st of October, 1992. And if we go to page 7 in e-court, down at the bottom there's a question by an individual, Tim Judah: "Two quick questions. You talked about terrorists, especially in SE and the connection was implicit but not explicit. Are the terrorists special militia, special police that you were referring to? That's the first question. And the second question: What are you going to do about it?" If we turn the page: "I know Tim Judah's quick questions. Your first question, are the terrorists the same as special militia, in many cases, yes. In many cases they seem to belong to gangs, who ... have moved in there from Serbia." Who controls the border between Sector East and Serbia, under the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR controls -- controls the movements of military personnel, arms ammunition, et cetera, et cetera, but there's movement of commerce so it's a complex question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: At some stage there was an attempt by the RSK authorities to set up border controls; isn't that right? And I should say as well. Set up border controls as well as the existing UNPROFOR controls?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is. But I'm not an expert on this topic, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: It's not really a question of expertise. It's just a question of memory?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So you do remember that that occurred at some point?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Any recollection of when that might have occurred for the first time that that was attempted?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm thinking sometime in late 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And, otherwise, and even not otherwise, even if there was also a border post set up by the local authorities, it's UNPROFOR, under the Vance Plan, that has responsibility to control that border.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: To control the movement of armed elements and the weapons of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And that might not include people who are members of gangs who cross the border without their weapons. Is that what you're entertaining the possibility of?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite possible people could come through if they were not armed and they were not uniformed, then they would be considered to be normal commerce. Civilian traffic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was it possible to get around the UNPROFOR controls in some way or another?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clearly it was. Because the Serb forces were able to move equipment, contraband quite successfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And according to Cedric Thornberry, gangs were also able to enter Sector East from Serbia, implicitly criminal gangs; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I mean, how they entered isn't specified.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 05268, please. I'm sorry, Mr. President, may I tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D93, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This is an UNPROFOR document dated the 5th of October, 1992. Military information summary from 25 September to 1st October 1992. Now, what I'm most interested in in this document is the annex which at page 19 in e-court. And there it says: "Border milicija, total STR: 1600 to 2.000 persons. HQ Erdut, COMD: Mr. Kostic." Any idea who Mr. Kostic is a reference to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we turn the page, we see in grand total that there are four border battalions. Gives their strengths, their locations. We don't need to go into that in detail. I just wanted you to have sight of the four battalions indicated. And then if we go to the next page, please. Now, here we have a reference to special purpose milicija, special milicija, and there are three headquarters indicated. And when you add up those numbers there, we see a strength of 260 to 330 men total. Do you see that. You don't need to do the math. I did the math, and I'm pretty sure it's accurate.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So you have a border police that is 1600 to 2.000 persons strong under the command of someone named Mr. Kostic according to this document and you have a special purpose milicija which has 260 to 330 men; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you remember that it was the border police that had by far the preponderance of strength amongst, let's say, and I'm searching for a term, a non-regular police. Was it the border police that was the -- that was the dominant -- numerically the dominant force, in your recollection and you may not recall?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall, but it wouldn't surprise me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Why not? You say it wouldn't surprise you. Do you have some indication in your mind as to why it is not surprising?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because a lot of the special police were deployed along the borders, in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So do I understand from that answer that you're saying that what this org chart is reflecting is the special purpose milicija who are not at the borders?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh. This is highly complex and I have great sympathy for the Bench because I spent two years dealing with this and never developed a full understanding of what forces were there. But I would say that this is quite deliberate. We weren't meant to understand it. They were camouflaged, hidden. They were meant to confuse so that they could retain force and do whatever they wanted without people really being able to do anything about it. It's -- this particular document here is an understanding of the police organisation at a point in time. There would be later documents which we find this information. This is very early in UNPROFOR's understanding of the situation in the UNPAs. Over time, it got better. But it was deliberately confusing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Just a couple of short questions, Brigadier, because we're at the break. This is October 1992, a good six months after the deployment, not early in the deployment unless you consider six months to be early.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe UNPROFOR took over in Sector East in June or mid-October -- mid-July, perhaps [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: No advance teams there from April?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: From March, in fact. The first people would have arrived in the UNPAs. But, as I say, there was a deliberate policy of obscuring the reality on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Except that Mr. Spanovic met on at least two occasions with Mr. Thornberry, the civil affairs co-ordinator or the civil affairs person, and set out, at least in Mr. Thornberry's words, a frank description of the forces?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, many things were said in those meetings, counsel, that were not true and many commitments were made which were not honoured. That's the reality of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gosnell. Brigadier, time for our first break. Thirty minutes. We'll come back at 11.00. The Court Usher will escort you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, I'm sorry to insist, and I'll tell you why. It's because I -- we have to eventually take measures, if necessary, for this afternoon. How long would you think you'll take and then I'll ask for the re-direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: There's a chance I might finish before the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And, if not then, then shortly thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, what is -- what do you think you will need in re-direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Currently I don't think any more than 15 minutes. So I think we're well within --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah. Nothing has to be done for the moment. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could we have 65 ter 1344; Defence tab 33. And while this is coming up, Brigadier, this is a letter from General Nambiar to Marrack Goulding dated the 9th of November, 1992, with an attachment and the attachment is a letter from Mr. Zecevic - it's possible we've seen this document before. I'm not sure - and the date of the letter is the 4th of November, 1992. If we could go to page -- page 2. It's not the same letter that we looked at previously from Mr. Zecevic. But you'll recall, Brigadier, that we did see a previous letter from Mr. Zecevic. And once again he appears to be reiterating his insistence of his interpretation of that provision of the Vance Plan. We won't revisit that issue. If we go over to page 3, in the same way we insisted that you answer whether you are capable of executing your responsibilities from the cited regulation to which we either got no answer or a negative answer. Nevertheless we continued with activities in the process of demilitarisation towards executing item possibly 15 of the Vance Plan, where we completed items A, B, C, while units addressed by item D were completely disbanded and demobilised. At the same time armed groups which might eventually be seen on the terrain are outside the composition of our militia units and are presenting to us at this moment a bigger problem than they are to you. Now I see you're shaking your head. I assume that you disagree with what he is saying or what is your reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just understand what groups he is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And by that you mean you don't understand how he is using the term "armed groups"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand which armed groups he is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But he is clearing indicating, is he not, that there is an authorised force of armed people and, in his view, armed groups that are outside of the composition of our militia units; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is consistent with many statements in many meetings I attended which said that it was beyond the control of the -- the person there because these were ill disciplined groups or uncontrolled groups or -- or whatever. There was wide acknowledgement, indeed. Sometimes uses an excuse that such groups existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, we're going to come eventually or shortly to the issue of responsibility for disbanding such groups. But for now we can say that there is at least in Mr. Zecevic's mind a distinction; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May I tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D94, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have D73, please, which is Prosecution tab 67.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This is again from General Nambiar to Mr. Goulding. Info Vance 30 November 1992. It says that: "Thornberry travelling to Knin to seek to repair some political bridges in poor condition in recent months. Four hours private discussion with Colonel Stojan Spanovic, minister of defence of RSK, then dinner with him and minister of energy, Bjegovic. The main direct consequence is that we are opening negotiations later this week with RSK on border controls." If we could turn the page, I'd like to focus in on the paragraph that I'm interested in your observations on. Paragraph 6: "We kept clear of displaced persons' issues on this occasion and said little about disarmament. But Spanovic volunteered that they were making a very big effort to clean up their act by arresting their bandits and making life hot for their gangsters especially in Sector East. Clearly very sensitive to this matter, now, he agreed precisely with our analysis, and felt that the deadline into anarchy line we have been publicly taking could destroy any residual credibility they may have." Let's just pause there. Did you observe that the Serb side understood that their credibility was being damaged by lack of security in the protected areas?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I -- I don't believe they saw that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So do you think that General Nambiar, who you previously described as extremely well-informed, I believe yesterday, in his face-to-face conversations with Mr. Spanovic, are you saying that he has gotten this wrong?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is Mr. Thornberry reporting on a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, let's go back to page 1. From Nambiar.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. But it's signed by Thornberry. The protocol was that your -- it's always from Nambiar, Zagreb, or wherever he happened to be, but releasing officer in this case is Thornberry. This would be, I believe, a record of Thornberry's conversation, without having the opportunity to read the whole document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What would Nambiar's role be in the drafting of a document of this nature where his name appears on the from line but then we see a signature such as this?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, without reading this whole document, counsel, you know, I can't refer to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let me just clarify then because there already is a confusion in my question. I'm not asking about this document. I'm asking your knowledge of general practice. If we have a document that in the from line is indicated to be from a person, in this case, Nambiar and it's signed -- let's take the specific example of Nambiar and Thornberry. It's from Nambiar. Thornberry' signature is there. What would you understand from general practice Nambiar's role in such a document would be?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's just a signal address. It's -- all correspondence going from UNPROFOR headquarters to UN New York should be from Nambiar and then you would recognise by the releasing officer, the person who signs it, who -- who -- probably who the author is or at least he is accepting responsibility for releasing that cable. But all correspondence going to New York should be Nambiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So do I understand correctly that that means Thornberry can't write directly to Goulding?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You understand correctly. Nambiar is the boss, and all communications should go through Nambiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Okay. So your view, understanding that you don't know the particularities about this document, is that it could likely have been created without any direct role by Nambiar?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, most certainly it could have gone to New York without Nambiar seeing it before it went. But he would see this document in his daily pile of papers and if he had a problem with it, after the event, then he would certainly raise that with the author and a correction would be made to New York. But there's a delegation of authority and there's trust involved in here between colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So the least that can be said is that there is a presumption that Nambiar agrees if we have a document of this nature; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Subject to there being no other communication, correspondence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let's now return to page 2, please. Now, and I want -- I'm focussing on the issue of their sensitivity as recorded in this document. Are you saying Thornberry has got it wrong?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm saying that he -- he is recorded here his record of a conversation that he's had. And this document does indicate that there's a genuine willingness of the Serb authorities to address a particular issue concerning security.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what this document says.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let's just leave aside the issue of the measures and whatever steps might be taken to restore security and let's focus on the issue of sensitivity. In other words whether this was a matter of concern to them. And I suggest what we have Thornberry saying is that he perceives that they are clearly very sensitive to it matter; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And he uses the expressing "now."

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Does that suggestion to you that there may have been at least in respect of Spanovic, as far as Thornberry concerned, an evolution?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was and there were further developments also in this conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And yet your previous answer was that you saw no evidence that your Serb interlocutors were sensitive to that issue. Is that -- is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I interpreted the question was, did I believe that the Serbs were concerned about their credibility on this matter, and my answer was, no, I didn't. Over my two years of experience, I believe they're quite insensitive to how they presented themselves to UNPROFOR and to the world through the media in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: In your view, during negotiations with UNPROFOR or other international interlocutors, you're saying that the Serb side was oblivious as to how these kind of events were affecting their negotiating position, their credibility, in the negotiations. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: My belief is that they were not aware how their stance on these matters presented to other people, to UNPROFOR, and to the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And I assume that also means they were oblivious to the fact that the Croatian side was using this information and evidence of -- of these events to maximum advantage in the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could see this, and they were quite frustrated by the situation, that the Croats were able to use perhaps the international media more effectively than the Serb people were. But the question -- my answer to your question remains the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: At -- do you attribute that to stupidity or callousness or what do you attribute that to? Because I have to say, I find that rather hard to understand.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't know in any way want to be insulting in my description here, but I believe it was ignorance of how these issues were played out in other forums outside of Serbia, outside the former Yugoslavia. I don't know that they were reading the media the way the rest of the world was. I don't know that they saw how their stance in the various negotiations in Geneva and other places played out, that they -- you know, the image they were presenting or they believe they were presenting was not the same as other observers interpreted it. Perhaps it was cultural. I'm not sure, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you attribute it to a lack of sophistication in understanding how these issues were manifestly playing out in the negotiations, as well as in the media?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't attribute to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 1324, please. Before I do turn to that document, was the view that you just expressed by, as far as you know, Mr. Thornberry himself in your conversations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So he didn't convey anything to you about this particular meeting that he describes in that document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I've seen this document. Mr. Thornberry attended many meetings. I saw many of the records of those meetings and we had many discussions. I mean, he expressed a level of frustration in dealing with the Serb authorities and trying to explain to them that it was in their best interests to perhaps modify their stance and their behaviour, and he felt that he was wasting his time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Actually, could I have 01307, please; Prosecution tab 65. This is a weekly situation assessment. It doesn't have the cover page that we often see with these documents, but it's dated the 7th of October, 1992. It appears to be the TO -- the COO.
