And down under item 5, the problem of the border police with Hungarian border has to be included in the overall demilitarisation plan. The only way to hinder terrorism is the disarmament and disabandonment of regional milicija. It has to be followed by disarmament of all civilians and the local milicija which is allowed to carry only side weapons. About 70 per cent of civilians possess weapons at home. I asked you about that yesterday. Does that jog your memory that that was the level of armament available at large in the civilian population at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think my answer yesterday was that I didn't know the precise percentage but it wouldn't surprise me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And am I right that one of the steps of the Vance Plan that you identified requires disarmament not only of armed groups but actually everyone?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Not very realistic, is it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's what the parties agreed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. Not very realistic, that was the question.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe if the parties had genuinely intended to carry out their agreement, then it was realistic, and it was quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And the parties didn't include anyone, include any authority from the -- what would later become the RSK, did it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it didn't. But it did have the most senior Serb political leader signed it. The document we've seen, a letter, from -- I think it was then-Vice-President Kosic, or, in reality, he was the acting president of Yugoslavia, and -- and there was also the oral agreement at least of President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have P2227.2168, which is Defence tab 52. It's also 01478, for the assistance of the Registry. Thank you very much. This is a fax dated the 8th of February, 1993, between UN CIVPOL entities. Item 3, on page 1: "Knin CIVPOL station reported that they had a patrol in the village of Vrpolje. They met local milicija who are guarding the residents of this village. The Croatian who were forced to leave their houses by the refugees are still leaving in the school, the milicija informs CIVPOL that they have three buses to transport Croatian people from that village but they didn't get the confirmation from Sibenik that the CA side is ready to accept them. There were no complaints from those Croatian people during this visit." Now this is the 8th of February, 1993. It's right after the incursion at Maslenica bridge. This is Sector South. Does that tell you anything about where the -- what's described here as refugees would have been from?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I -- my reading of this document is that they're Croatian refugees from this village in Sector South. They had been evicted by, I presume, Serb refugees from other areas, and they're living in the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What other areas would those Serb refugees have been from, at this date, in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could have come from Bosnia, perhaps other areas of Croatia. Could have come from redistribution of refugees within the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Nothing to do with the week-long offensive by the Croatian army in the Benkovac area?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I included that. I said they could have come from Croatia. But they could have come from any of these other places too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Page 2: "During the meeting, OPS officer was introduced to the new police for Knin and Sector South, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I have no page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. It's coming up.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's up. But which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The very last paragraph there.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: "During the meeting, OPS off was introduced to the new chief of police for Knin and Sector South, Mr. Nebojsa Pavkovic. He is also the assistant of Minister Milan Martic. This man will be chief until Mr. Ilija Prijic come back. He was informed about all the problems and he is ready to help us and to have a very good co-operation but it is very difficult to have co-operation now because of the war situation." In general terms isn't what is going on here is there are, what I suggest, refugees who have come from fighting in the Benkovac area. They're angry, having just been forced out of their homes. They've gone to another location and started terrorising Croat civilians who then fled to a school where they are being protected by the local police. Does that fairly summarise what's in this document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have only read two very short paragraphs in this document. I don't see any reference there to Maslenica or, indeed, that the refugees came from there. You're suggesting it. It may have come from there and it may be a reasonable suggestion, but it's also possible that the refugees referred to earlier in this document could have come from anywhere. It's not -- without a thorough reading of the document I can't really agree or disagree with you, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, there's a reference there to the war situation apparently as being the source of the problems; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the last paragraph, it says the war situation makes the situation difficult. It doesn't refer at all to the question of the refugees in the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we go to the next page, please. The second paragraph: "A common problem at present is that local Croats are still being forced out of their houses an apartments by both newly arriving refugees and by local opportunists. Local authorities appear powerless to stop this." Now let me ask you this general question: Did you know that internally displaced persons, Serbs from parts of Croatia that were pushed into the protected areas, were they particularly militant and extremist, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, there was -- they were a general cross-section of the community.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you see this document at the time, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll be unlikely to see this. This is an internal police document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So is it fair to say you didn't review any police documents at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I saw police documents which were on a school of float, which is a lot of documentation which may be of interest but it's not specifically referred to me for an action, and I therefore have the opportunity to have a general read of this. This is the quite common in military organisations that if you're not the action officer, you -- you have the opportunity to read general correspondence passing through the headquarters. Now this type of report may or may not be on the float if it is considered to be of interest. I can't say I never read reports. I have no recollection of reading this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You weren't playing close attention to police reports because it wasn't within your area of responsibility; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was within my general area of interest rather than my specific area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So you didn't rigorously or closely examine such reports during the course of your time there; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, back in January 1992, when you first met Mr. Hadzic, the JNA was still on the ground in Sector East; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: How many times did you visit Sector East between the time you arrived in the former Yugoslavia and the time that you were deployed to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two or three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And during those two or three times, did you observe that the JNA was in control of the territory of what would become Sector East?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And what makes you say that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were evident by their uniforms and their deployment. The people I met were JNA officers who claimed to be in control of the area and to be the authority in the area at that time, the practical authority. I don't recall meeting, in that time-frame, any of the political authorities. I may have, but I don't remember it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were they controlling the -- as far as you could observe, the crossing points between Serbia and Sector East?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were you able to observe whether they were exercising authority over all - and I mean all - irregular forces in Sector East; i.e., non-JNA.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they were, but on occasions when we raised our concern about cease-fire violations, they would often attribute these to "uncontrolled" elements?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now as a military man, if you have a militia fighting alongside you, for example, in Vietnam or anywhere else, Lebanon, from your past experience, you have an obligation as commander in that area to subordinate that irregular group, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And to oblige them to comply with the provisions, for example, of any cease-fire agreements; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends upon the command relationships. Military forces are deployed. You are told usually in writing who your boss is and what your relationship is with other forces in the area, what your responsibility is to supervise them and to support them. There are various terms like under command, in support, under command, less administration, et cetera. These are technical military terms but soldiers quite clearly understand that if you're deployed in the line what your relationship is with another units. There is no ambiguity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And not only on the line, in the depth of the territory; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was there any discussion within UNPROFOR - and I ask you this as someone who would be very familiar with these issues - whether after the declaration of independence by Croatia that the JNA should be considered an army of occupation under the Law of Armed Conflict?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall such a technical discussion, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 695, please. Do you remember who signed the first cease-fire agreement, the Geneva Accord, of 23rd November 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, this is a version of the Geneva Accord. Unfortunately, it's not the original version. But it does indicate there that it's signed by Tudjman, Milosevic, Kadijevic and Vance. Seeing this, does that in any way refresh your memory that those were the signatories?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've not seen this document before. And to be honest, cease-fires or arrangements for cease-fires before the 2nd of January were of very little interest because there were so many cease-fires that were not respected that they were irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, I suggest this one was not irrelevant because this is the one that ultimately took hold.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding was that -- the document signed on 2nd of January in Sarajevo was -- was the cease-fire that was -- the important one in terms of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Subpart (c) of this, "They will immediately," and "they" is the undersigned: "They will immediately instruct all units under their command and control or political influence to observe an unconditional cease-fire with effect from tomorrow, 24 November, and they will make sure that any paramilitary or irregular units not formally under their command, control, or political influence also observe the cease-fire from that date ..." Now do you agree with me that that imposes very categorically an obligation on the JNA to enforce the cease-fire, if necessary, by enforcing it against all irregular elements in Sector East and -- and elsewhere in the protected areas?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, as a military man and as a member of UNPROFOR, can you think of why it would be necessary to have the JNA as a separate party to such agreements? My point being why not just have Milosevic sign?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my military culture and my political upbringing, the political authority speaks for the military. This must have been perceived by all parties concerned that the military needed to be included in it, otherwise it might not happen. But it's not part of my culture.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And can you help us understand why they wouldn't have had the most senior official in the rump Presidency of the SFRY sign the document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean, you're asking me about a document that existed, discussions that took place, considerations that were taken in account two months before I became involved in this conflict at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Would you agree with me -- and this doesn't flow direct from the demilitarisation agreement that is on the screen but it may flow from the general principle that you articulated earlier. Would you agree with me that it is for the military force in an area of responsibility and territorial control of an area of responsibility to prevent aligned or allied forces operating in that area from committing crimes?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have L2, please. And if we could please turn to page 14. Again, Brigadier, this is the bundle of documents containing the Vance Plan. And actually we should start on page 13. Now, when do you say that the Vance Plan was agreed to, the date?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The cease-fire was signed on the 2nd of January. That's what I understand. That's why UNMLOY was deployed to monitor and report on that cease-fire. My understanding is that the Vance Plan was not finally accepted until sometime after Mr. Goulding's visit in late January to -- to -- to the area, that there was an assurance given by all parties concerned that they would honour the agreement. So when it was signed, I don't really understand, but it was the Secretary-General's -- Secretary-General's concern that the parties were genuinely committed to the plan that necessitated Mr. Goulding's visit and it was based on the assurances given at that visit and immediately afterwards that the decision was made to go ahead with the deployment of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, the provision and I think this is completely uncontested that this is the applicable provision that was agreed to, paragraph 15, describing demilitarisation of the UNPAs. On the basis of the agreed timetables, demilitarisation would be implemented as rapidly as possible in the following ways [sic]: (a) is, I think, self-ex explanatory; (b) is self explanatory. If we can turn the page. Likewise, (c) fairly clear; and there's (d): "All paramilitary, irregular or volunteer units or personnel would either be withdrawn from the UNPAs, or, if resident in them, be disbanded and demobilised." Now, let's take January 30th as a reference point. On January 30th, that is before Sector East is a part of the RSK and while, according to you, the JNA is still in territorial control of Sector East prior to the assumption of responsibility by UNPROFOR, for that matter even the arrival of anyone from UNPROFOR, who has the responsibility to enforce paragraph (d)?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Why don't you say the local authorities have that responsibility?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the military were in control, stated they were in control and accepted responsibility for what was happening in that area in the negotiations and in the discussions that I had with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Would it be your view that this provision means that they are required to accomplish that obligation prior to their withdrawal from Sector East and the other protected areas?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not -- not necessarily. The sequence there suggests that the first thing to happen was the withdrawal of the JNA. That's the sequence laid out in the report there. And there was to be subsequent demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Are you implying that (a), (b), (c), and (d) were meant to be effectuated sequentially?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They would happen in some cases at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You say in some cases and you've also said that the obligation is on the JNA to enforce subparagraph (d), so doesn't that mean that (d) is going to happen before (a)?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps if would happen at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now let's say as of the withdrawal date or at the moment that the JNA withdraws from Sector East, who inherits the obligation under -- or if anyone at all, maybe no one inherits. But what happens to the obligation in 15 (d) according to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it passes to the senior political leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Of what?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the -- of the Sector East.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Which, on January 30th, was the -- well, I'm sorry, let me -- let me correct myself. On January 30th we have the JNA and sometime in --

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: February.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes. And sometime in the summer or late spring we have the withdrawal of the JNA. So you would locate in time the occurrence of the obligation on the local authorities as being coincident with the withdrawal of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that if the JNA has completely effected its withdrawal and in that process has left behind some armed elements that it is not overseeing the withdrawal of or has been unable to do so, that once it is out of that area, that responsibility passes to the senior political leadership by default.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And prior to the withdrawal of the JNA, that is while it is still in territorial control of the area, in addition to the obligation under paragraph (d), would you agree that they have a -- a general obligation, again based on the principles we've previously discussed, to prevent those allied forces from committing crimes?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, you say that it's the obligation of the senior political authorities upon the departure of the JNA to effectuate subparagraph (d), and down at the bottom of the page, we have a definition of the forces that are at the disposal of local authorities. And it says: "The maintenance of public order in the UNPAs would be the responsibility of local police forces who would carry only side-arms ... the local police forces would be responsible to the existing opstina councils in the UNPAs. Any existing regional police structures would remain in place, provided that they were consistent with the principle described above concerning the national composition of the local police force [sic]." Now, given that that's the only force that's at the disposal under the Vance Plan of the local authorities, how are they supposed to carry out the obligation in subparagraph (d)?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police forces in Sector East, after the withdrawal of the JNA, represented some thousands of people quite heavily armed, quite capable of dealing with relatively small but disruptive armed elements. There were plenty of resources available to the political authorities if they're given adequate direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And the view of UNPROFOR was that all those forces were illegal; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which forces are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What you described in your previous answer as the police forces in Sector East.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly there were some thousands of normal policemen as we have in any society. And there were a number of special police that's acknowledged in paragraph 19 that existed that could have been called upon to exist. It says existing police structures, which provides for the fact that there may have been other police but they would be of a particular composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President, did I misstate something from the previous answer or is there a confusion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's the -- I think it's the qualification as illegal. Is that part of the witness's answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Not that particular answer but we've heard, I believe, a number of answers that indicated that earlier in the testimony. Let me try to rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: They would be - am I right - in your view, illegal if they were armed with long-barrelled weapons, any police forces, whether they be local or regional?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I'm not sure what the Bench might interpret the word "illegal" to mean. What I'm saying in my evidence, Your Honour, is that these people were in breach of the Vance Plan agreements. They're violations of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let's go to page 5 of L2, please. Now this is from the Secretary-General's report that accompanies the agreement and it says there in the second-last sentence of paragraph 12 and I hope we can zoom in. Well, let's go back a couple of sentences even. It says: "On this basis, United Nations troops and police monitors would be deployed in these areas, which would be designated as United Nations Protected Areas. They would be demilitarised and all armed forces in them would be either withdrawn or disbanded. The role of the United Nations troops would be to ensure that the areas remained demilitarised and that all persons residing in them were protected from fear of armed attack. The role of the United Nations police monitors would be to ensure that the local police forces carried out their duties without discriminating against persons of any nationality or abusing anyone's ... rights." This is the key sentence, I say. "As the United Nations force assumed its responsibilities in the UNPAs all of the JNA forces deployed elsewhere in Croatia would be located outside the republic." Can you see any indication in that paragraph that it appears to be UNPROFOR that is the force that is the successor to the JNA in terms of responsibilities under the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read the sentence -- the critical sentence here is that -- it's the third sentence which states clearly the role of the United Nations would be to ensure the areas remained demilitarised. That is, UNPROFOR would inherit a security situation in the UNPAs that was completely demobilised and UNPROFOR would then be responsible for maintaining or for protecting people within the UNPAs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let me try to first pin down the scope of that obligation. The word "remained," are you suggesting and I have heard your answers from the last two days, but are you suggesting that the areas had to be completely denuded of arms, completely demilitarised before the obligation to prevent remilitarisation exists, or would you agree that this obligation implies blocking any reinsertion of arms into the protected areas after UNPROFOR takes over?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's both. It should be demilitarised and UNPROFOR should prevent the reinsertion of military force.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And in the event the first doesn't happen and if 70 per cent of the population at least have arms, we know that that simply is not going to happen, if the first doesn't happen, the second obligation still exists; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've covered this several times in the last couple of days, counsel. My contention is that it was a deliberate centrally conceived managed policy not to disarm, to circumvent the provisions of the Vance agreement. It was deliberate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You've not answered my question.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, would you restate it then, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I can just repeat it.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: It says -- the question was: If the first doesn't happen, if there is not absolute and complete demilitarisation of the sectors by the time UNPROFOR takes over, doesn't UNPROFOR still have that obligation to prevent the reinsertion of arms into the sectors?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Is it your view that -- UNPROFOR infantry has no role in policing and maintaining internal security in the protected areas under the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were there to foster a safe and secure environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And that included -- as a sovereign state would control its boundaries, that included UNPROFOR exercising territorial control to the extent at least of manning the -- what I don't want to called border posts between Serbia and Sector East but the crossing points?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UN established control points to prevent the reintroduction or the movement of military force within the UNPA. That was their purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And UNPROFOR undertook many efforts to, as best it could, given the resources available, maintain security in the protected areas; right? And by "security," I'm referring here to violence by individuals against other individuals inside the protected areas.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But that -- it's an issue of when is it law and order and when is it sort of a military security issue. Depends upon the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, one of the aspects of the process that you noted about refugees was that they were often occupied in vacated homes. And you said a couple of different things about that. On the one hand, you said, at 7905, that people had to have somewhere to leave. But then at 7495, you said, that you considered this to be, I believe -- if I may just have a moment. Yes, you said that you merely commented that in some cases they were being once vacated occupied by Serb refugees from other areas. Is your view that those refugees were forcing merely by virtue of living in the houses that were vacated, did you view that as a process of forcing out the previous inhabitants or are those two phenomena at least in particular circumstances separate?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some cases, it was separate. In other cases, it was entirely related.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 05230, please, which is Prosecution tab 157. Do you know that the local authorities, the RSK authorities, were careful to ensure that, to the extent that they could enforce this, that those who inhabited vacated houses understood that it was only a temporary measure?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm unaware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This is a letter from Mr. Thornberry to Mr. Susa, 27 August, and Mr. Thornberry is complaining about individuals having their property confiscated. And then if we turn over to page 4. There should be a translation attached.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May I inquire of the Registry how many pages this document has?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Three page, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The document appears not to have the translation, at least the version I have. And I'm just going to skip the document and move on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The translation seems to be on the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Brigadier, you said that you --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Did you hear the interpreter's intervention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have a translation on the left-hand page of my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes, that's it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And if we can go down to the bottom, we have Mr. Susa responding to this letter from Mr. Thornberry and he says he admits that there is a provision of the criminal code that permits such confiscation, but he says that it cannot be ordered without a court order. And then at the bottom he says: "No cases in which property confiscation has been pronounced as an additional sentence has been registered so far." If we turn the page: "Please do not be confused by the fact that a certain number of individuals banished from the territory of the Republic of Croatia has moved into buildings in the RSK [sic] which had previously been abandoned for various reasons by their owns. This measure - temporarily moving in, primarily as a humanitarian aspect, without the right of the temporary inhabitants to treat the property as their own." That's a complete sentence. Not entirely grammatical. But would you agree that -- or did you ever hear that in fact this was what the Serb policy or position was in respect of this accommodation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: In your testimony you said that you saw a mosque that was destroyed in Sector North; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of the town?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you remember roughly where it was geographically?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somewhere to the west of Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: West of Bihac?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Across the border from Bosnia in Croatia or in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the UNPA.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: My understanding is that there was no mosque in that area. Are you sure that you weren't in Bosnia at this time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: It's possible your recollection is mistaken?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. But the location might -- might be an error in recollection but not the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Brigadier, thank you very much for your time, for coming here.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, those are my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gosnell. Mr. Olmsted, I see the time. I would suggest we take the break now and come back at 12.40, in 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That works with me, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wilson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Brigadier, you stated during cross-examination that UNPROFOR had the responsibility to control the borders in the UNPAs to prevent the reinstatement of arms into the sectors. Now, we touched on this during direct examination a bit, but can you tell us why UNPROFOR was not able to carry out this particular part of its mandate.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the -- firstly a lot of the arms remained hidden within the area. Secondly, because they were moved by whomever around the UN control points. There was a deliberate attempt to move points around. In some cases, people forced their way through UN control points and the UN were unable to stop them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, I think Mr. Gosnell was referring you to a chart that represented there were perhaps even thousands of, quote/unquote, border, RSK border police. Were these border police assisting UNPROFOR with the task of controlling the borders of the UNPAs?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean by assisting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I mean were they helping protect the borders, to prevent these -- prevent this reinstatement of arms at the borders. Were they helping UNPROFOR carry out its mandate?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding from reports is that in some cases they were in effect denying entry into the area and in other cases they were facilitating it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And with regard to the latter, with regard to facilitating it, did this cause a significant problem for UNPROFOR in carrying out its mandate?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It contributed to the unstable threatening environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You were also asked during cross-examination a number of questions about the JNA's responsibilities, both in the pre-Vance Plan period, as well as under the Vance Plan. Now, are you familiar with the military laws that applied to the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And do you have actual knowledge with regard to the organisation and the chain of command of -- let's take Territorial Defence units that were operating in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we did get an answer. Yes, we did. I apologise. And what about other let's call them non-JNA forces that were operating in the Serb-controlled areas of Croatia? Did you have any understanding particularly at the early phase, January, February, March 1992, with regard to their chain of command and who they reported to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: We believe they were controlled from authorities in Belgrade. That's as much detail as I was aware of at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So do you know what degree the local authorities - and when I say "local authorities," I mean the authorities that eventually became the RSK government - do you know what powers, authorities, influence they exercised over these non-JNA units, armed units that were operating in these areas?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they at least condoned their deployment. I'm not aware of the exact level of control or effectiveness of control they had over them. I understood in many ways they were quite independent and could do as they wished.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And in some cases they were independent of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were they, in some cases, independent of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'll even say it broadly. Who are they independent of?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe they were responsive to some direction from authorities in Belgrade, and they may or may have not have responded to whoever was the local authority as it suited them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Under the Vance Plan, was it only the JNA who had responsibility for demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The militias, whoever controlled them, that is, the territorial forces or the TDF, also had to disarm. And whoever was responsible for them had to ensure that it was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did the JNA have the sole responsibility to reign in the local armed forces, the TOs, or whatever you want to call them, and to prevent their crimes?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe while the JNA was occupying the UNPAs, they did have, as an occupying force, the ultimate legal responsibility to control all elements within that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did they share that responsibility with anyone?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Would you be able to comment on what the role of the local authorities would be with regard to those crimes?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The crimes?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The crimes committed by these local forces. I'm not talking about JNA forces. I'm talking about TO units, or members of TO units or members of -- of other local armed forces that were operating in these Serb-controlled areas of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: At what point in time?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I'm talking about before the JNA withdrew.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They may have some authority or influence over them, but ultimately I believe it is the occupying military power who has the responsibility for the control of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell was raising some issues regarding the cease-fire agreement that was -- the Geneva Accord, I think it was referred to, from November of 1991. But I want to ask you about the Vance Plan. Did anyone actually sign the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The plan was attached to a report by the Secretary-General from December 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It wasn't a -- a treaty or a document that was signed by any parties.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was the role of Mr. Goulding in January 1992? What was his -- his chief aim? You talked about a number of meetings he was holding. What was he trying to do?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was trying to achieve a firm assurance from all of the responsible parties that they supported and would implement all of the provisions of the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And again I think you touched on this in direct examination, but what was the position that Mr. Hadzic took with regard to the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he accepted the Vance Plan but pointed out some of the difficulties; in particular, the difficulty of two nations of Croats and Serbs living together in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And the latter issue was the political issue, if I understand it correctly.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But he broadly accepted the Vance Plan. He did not object to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's look at 65 ter 3054. This is tab 125. This is a -- an UNPROFOR weekly situation assessment dated 11 November 1992. And if we could turn to page 3 and go to the bottom, we see it states: "Declaration of RSK on meeting organised on 7 November 1992 that pink zone areas belong to Krajina. Therefore, no Croatian authorities will be allowed to take over or part in control." And if turn the page, the part I'm particularly interested in says: "... second declaration was that RSK believes to be independent and do not recognise the Vance Plan because it never has been signed by anyone from RSK government." I'm particularly interested in the second declaration about not signing the Vance Plan. What do you make of this argument being made in November of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, objection. If this document hasn't been used up until this time, because I would say that it exceeds the scope of a re-direct. Just embarks into additional evidence -- there is no lack of clarity that has been suggested in the cross or -- so I think this would set a very bad precedent if we just open the door to additional documents being used on re-direct unless there's some particular reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. President, this goes to the issue which Mr. Gosnell spent a significant amount of time on is with regard to the signing of these agreements and what that entailed, and I'm pursuing this issue of the lack of signatures on, in particular, the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Brigadier, I just want, again, to focus your attention on the issue of -- of the statement or the declaration that was made with regard to the non-signing of the Vance Plan, and if you could give us what you make of this kind of argument being made in November of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I wouldn't have placed any great weight on that report. It is just another statement made by somebody or other. There's no accountability usually associated with these sort of statements. It's perhaps a negotiation that was an attempt to delay or obscure. It's ... it's a meaningless statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Does it surprise you that the RSK would be making such a declaration in November 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And I mean, as -- as time went on, there were many qualifications about the Vance Plan, what was supported and what wasn't, what they thought they meant, and what they didn't. It was all meaningless sort of chatter delaying the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2875, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have on the screen P2179.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And earlier today you were shown this UNPROFOR military information summary dated 25 August 1992. And if we could turn to page 4 of the document. If we could focus in on Sector East. You recall, this is the document that Defence counsel drew your attention to, the report from Sector East regarding a killing incident. Now, if we could just turn to page 7 -- well, first of all, before we do that, after receiving a report such as this, Brigadier, what was the standard practice for UNPROFOR to verify this incident? Would they look into it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would. But ultimately this is a police function. If -- reading that report as it existed, it doesn't say that the firing came from outside the UNPA or this was an incursion by Croat forces. So could have been anybody, as I read that report, and which would suggest to me it's a law and order issue. That might be clear if I looked at a map and saw exactly where these vicinities -- these localities are.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You might be able to get some clarity if we look at page 7 of the report. And if we look under the 14th of August, 1992, item 4, we actually see some additional information that was acquired the next day. And it says: "In respect of the shooting of Serb farmers by CA," which I think there's no dispute, that's Croatian army, "near Markusica on 13 August, it has been learned that they first crossed the CFL," confrontation line, "there on 12 August. They were warned not to return, but did so on 13 August carrying with them grenades and SA," which, Brigadier, I think is a small arms?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: "It is believed that when the Croatian army attempted to arrest them, the Serbs opened fired [sic] which the Croatian army returned. Three Serb men and one woman were killed and one woman was wounded." Then it talks about the -- there must have been others who came across the border at the same time because it says 19 were arrested and it talks about their release. Now does this add clarity, with regard to this particular incident, in which local Serbs crossed the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I interpret that that the Croatians have crossed the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So you're saying that the -- how you read it, the Croatian army crossed and they were warned by the local Serbs not to return and they crossed again and then the Serbs approached them with grenades?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then the -- that's the way I'm reading it. Perhaps I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay. That's not how I would read it but I think that's fair enough. We'll leave that to argument. I think we'll just leave it at that. But, anyway, this is, Brigadier, an example of following up and looking more into the matter to see whether it is an issue with regard to the Vance Plan or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I don't even see a question there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Was there? Was there a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yeah. Is this an example of them following up into this matter. But I can withdraw the question. It's not that important. I think it speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yesterday it was put to you repeatedly that the Serbs did not demilitarise because of the concerns about the security threat by the Croatian army. And at one point, I believe this is at transcript page 7542, you responded that both sides got what they deserved. If we could look at 65 ter 5187. And while that's coming up, Brigadier, can I ask you: Did local Serb armed forces in certain situations engage in activities that may have provoked the Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I can't recall --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Objection. That's leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In this case, Your Honours, I don't think it is because it doesn't suggest any answer to my question. It's whether they did or they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, merely using the word provoking insinuates an answer, and that makes it leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's say, did the Serb armed forces engage in any activities that may have caused the Croatian forces on occasion to respond militarily?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: On many occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we look at this document in front of us, we have a -- looks like -- appears to be a situation report. The date is difficult to read but if we look at the upper right-hand corner we can see that it's 17 of June, 1992. And we can see that also at the very bottom where there's a signature. It has 17 June, 1992. And this reports: "Real danger was creating to the whole peacekeeping operation in our sector. Motor/shooting, organised by local militia, direction Vinkovci, forced the Croatian side to make a claim to us and warn that in case of the next opening fire from high calibres by JNA side, the Croatian army side will bring all their heavy weapons back to the region." What can you tell us about such incidents?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite common.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2876, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yesterday at transcript page, I believe, it's 7537, you were asked whether UNPROFOR was able to identify perpetrators of crimes against the non-Serbs. And I think you testified that you were aware of examples of such cases.

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember reports which actually named individuals and, in fact, said that they were known to have committed previous crimes, were known by the UN police to have committed previous crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And were those cases reported to the local police?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was done with them, based upon the information you had?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that, in most cases, no action was taken against these individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have on the screen, 65 ter 1301. And what we have in front of us is an International Conference of the Former Yugoslavia report dated 3 October 1992 from Cyrus Vance to the Secretary-General. And it appears to be, and Defence counsel will correct me if I'm wrong, a report on a meeting held with top Yugoslav officials. I think President Milosevic is mentioned there, as well as General Panic, along in the document. But what I want to draw your attention is -- is -- is page 4 of document, which is a section that deals with the situation on the UNPAs which was discussed at this meeting. And it ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, we have the right page now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And it states: "UNPROFOR is getting little or no co-operation in these regions and did not have sufficient strength to enforce the disbanding of these units." I think that relates to something that I'm not interested in at this point. The next sentence I am, however. It says: "However they had advised the local authorities of known criminals but nothing was done to apprehend and punish them." Is that consistent with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2877.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And finally along this same line you were asked a number of questions regarding the police and their function. And I want to return one last time to 65 ter 3624, which I think has been admitted into evidence now. This is the -- it's P2848. And it's the Secretary-General report for the 28th of September, 1992. And if we could turn to page 5. And if we could focus in on paragraph 17. We can see that this is a paragraph concerning the regular civil police force operating in the UNPAs. And the sentence I'm interested in is: "Some professional police chiefs have been dismissed and replaced by extremists who know nothing of police work, but a great deal about intimidation." What's your assessment of that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN BRIAN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's consistent with reports and discussions at that time, within the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Brigadier, is this the end of your testimony. Thank you again for coming to The Hague to assist the Tribunal. You are now released as a witness, and we wish you a safe journey back home. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Nothing else?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We wish you a safe weekend. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 26th day of August, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.13 p.m.,
